newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl sees Berlin chancellery at Europe's centre.
newsitem.headline: Kohl sees Berlin chancellery at Europe's centre.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Tuesday Germany's new chancellery near the Reichstag in Berlin would be a modest building reflecting "a relaxed self-confident" nation at Europe's centre in the next century.
When the boxy modern complex is finished in late 1999, he said at the groundbreaking ceremony, "Berlin will be at the centre of the future Europe, not on its edge."

By that time, he added, the European Union would be negotiating entry terms with eastern European countries which have sought to join the western community since the East-West divide ended with the Berlin Wall's fall in 1989.

Kohl said the 400-million mark ($240 million) complex, one of the last major building projects in the booming capital, would stand in an area symbolising all the "splendour and hubris, destruction and recommencement" of recent German history.

Whipped by an icy wind, Kohl said the H-shaped building -- with a large central cube for the chancellor's offices and two long wings for his staff -- would be a modest and dignified "visiting card" to show off to visiting foreign leaders.
"At the end of this century, which has given us so many chances, we Germans have all the reason to be modest now," said Kohl, 66, the longest-serving post-war chancellor.
At a news conference afterwards, Kohl declined to answer persistent questions on whether he planned to run for reelection in 1998 and become the first chancellor to use the new building.

He also joked about his decision to have the State Council Building -- the former seat of East Germany's presidency under Erich Honecker -- be used as a temporary chancellery if the new building is not ready on time.
"In my wildest dreams, I never thought I'd have an office in that building," he laughed, adding: "I have no worries about any ghosts there."

At the groundbreaking ceremony, watched over by workers in their bulldozers and steam shovels, Kohl lifted three scoops of dirt from ground which had to be softened up in advance because freezing temperatures and biting winds had hardened it.
The ceremony took place in a tree-lined field 500 metres (yards) west of the Reichstag, gutted by construction workers racing to renovate the building before 1999.

"We hope for a good and peaceful future here," Kohl said, referring to the immediate area, which saw fierce fighting in the closing days of World War Two. "In 1945 this area was in ruins. We hope that ruins will never again result from German polices."

The complex, at a bend in the Spree River with a clear view of the Reichstag, will be Berlin's third chancellery this century. Until the 1930s, chancellors used Bismarck's offices in the nearby Wilhelmstrasse, close to where Hitler built his New Reich Chancellery, destroyed in World War Two.
"The design radiates a relaxed self-confidence," Kohl said in his speech. "It unites modesty with dignity."
Kohl said united Germany was already becoming an important stopover point for world leaders and that trend would continue.
"We can already see in Bonn that Germany is one of the most visited places (for world leaders)," Kohl said. "It is one of the two or three world capitals with the most official visits."

The groundbreaking for the chancellery marked a symbolic point-of-no-return for the government's move from the former western capital of Bonn. Parliament voted in 1991 to move to Berlin but planning feuds brought long delays.
"It is now clear that all the talk about deadlines will now be confined to the history books," said Berlin Mayor Eberhard Diepgen. "The decision is made, the deadlines will be met."
Renovation work is under way in former East German ministry buildings which will house their all-German equivalents from 1999.
